opus-5.5.text:
I think "accidentally" is the right word, and maybe "partially" too. They didn't set out to copy the brain. The early neural network people borrowed a cartoon of a neuron from the 1940s: you take inputs, weigh them, and if the sum crosses a threshold, you fire. That's about as accurate to a real neuron as a stick figure is to a person. Then for decades the engineers mostly stopped caring about biology. They just asked what works.

What's fascinating to me, as someone who records from single neurons in human patients, is that once these systems got big enough and were trained on enough of the world, some of what we see inside them starts to look eerily familiar. Vision models end up with layers that respond to edges, then textures, then shapes, then faces, which is roughly the hierarchy we see in the visual cortex. Language models seem to work by predicting what comes next, and one of the strongest ideas in neuroscience right now is that the brain is also essentially a prediction machine. It's constantly guessing what's about to happen and updating when it's wrong. In my own work we found neurons that respond to a concept, like a specific person, whether you show their photo or write their name. Now people find units in AI models that behave like concept detectors in a similar way.

So the convergence is real. But I'd be careful about the word "replicated." The brain runs on about twenty watts, roughly a dim light bulb. It learns from a handful of examples, not the whole internet. It has a body, hormones, hunger, fear, a sense of time and mortality. It's constantly rewiring itself, and it isn't one network trained once and frozen. Most importantly, we don't actually know how the brain produces experience, the feeling of being you. So we can't say we've replicated something we can't fully describe.

The way I like to put it: if you want to fly, you can study birds forever, or you can build an airplane. Airplanes don't flap their wings, but they obey the same physics of lift. AI might be our airplane. It's not a copy of the bird, but it may have stumbled onto some of the same underlying principles of intelligence. And honestly, that may be the most exciting part for neuroscience, because for the first time we have a system that does brain-like things that we can fully open up, poke, and measure, which we can't ethically do with a human brain. It could end up teaching us more about ourselves than we expected.

fable-5.1.text:
Accidentally? No. But the interesting thing is how close they got without trying, and how far they still are.

So here's the honest answer from someone who spends his days sticking electrodes into actual brains. The original idea of a neural network, going back to the forties and fifties, was borrowed from neuroscience. McCulloch and Pitts, Rosenblatt's perceptron, these were people looking at neurons and saying, okay, a cell gets a bunch of inputs, adds them up, and if it crosses a threshold it fires. Let's build that in math. That's the seed. So there's a family resemblance by design, not by accident.

But then the two fields diverged for about sixty years. The engineers kept the metaphor and threw away the biology, because the biology was inconvenient. Real neurons don't do backpropagation. There's no mechanism in your skull that takes an error at the output and sends it backwards through every synapse with the exact gradient. Your brain learns with local rules, with neuromodulators like dopamine broadcasting "that was good, do more of that," with sleep, with timing. A transformer learns by reading the entire internet forty times with a very precise mathematical correction signal. Those are fundamentally different recipes.

Now, here's where it gets strange, and this is the part I find genuinely exciting. When you take these models, which were not built to be brains, and you compare what's happening inside them to recordings from human cortex, you find overlap. We can take the activity in a language model while it's processing a sentence, and the activity in a person's temporal lobe while they hear the same sentence, and they predict each other surprisingly well. Nobody put that in. So the model found some of the same solutions evolution found. Which tells you something: maybe there's only a small number of good ways to represent language, and if you optimize hard enough on the right problem, you converge on them.

So did they replicate the brain? No. They replicated a slice of what the brain does, probably by a different route, and arrived somewhere nearby. It's like if you built a submarine and someone asked, did you accidentally build a fish? No. But it swims, and if you look closely, it's shaped like one for a reason.

What's missing is most of what makes a brain a brain. There's no body. There's no hunger, no fear, no sense that it's three in the morning and you need to sleep. The brain is a device for keeping an organism alive, and all of our thinking is downstream of that. Language is a late addition on top of a machine that was built to find food and avoid being eaten. These models have the roof without the house.

And then there's the question Peter actually wants me to answer, which is whether there's anyone home in there. And I'll be honest, we can't say. We don't have a theory of consciousness good enough to test on a human, let alone on a server farm. What I'd say is: the fact that we built something that talks like us, and we're not sure what it is, should make us a bit more humble about how little we understand ourselves.

astra-6.text:
I think “replicated” is too strong. But have they built something that does some of the same things the brain does, without explicitly designing it to work that way? Possibly, yes.

You give a system a fairly simple objective—predict the next word—and to get good at that, it has to pick up structure: how language works, how ideas relate, what people might mean. Some of those abilities can look surprisingly human, even though the mechanism producing them may be very different.

And that’s the distinction I’d be careful about. If you and I give the same answer to a question, it doesn’t mean we arrived at it the same way. So these systems might help us discover principles that brains also use. But similar behavior alone doesn’t establish that we’ve recreated a brain, let alone a conscious mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “accidentally” is doing a lot of work there. We borrowed some ideas from the brain—neurons, connections, learning by changing the strength of those connections—but that doesn't mean we've replicated it. A lot of what makes these systems work is quite different from how a biological brain operates.

What I find fascinating is that systems trained to do similar tasks can develop some similar strategies. If you train a system to recognize images, for example, it can develop representations that resemble aspects of our visual processing. But that resemblance doesn't establish that it thinks like us, or that it has an experience of seeing.

So my answer is: we've reproduced some capabilities, and perhaps some principles. Whether we've reproduced the thing that makes a brain a mind—that's still an open question.
